a66.speaker: William Ruto, President of Kenya (summit co-chair)
a66.speech: "The situation in eastern DRC is dire. It has led to a humanitarian crisis that has taken countless lives, and we must act now," said President Ruto during the opening session. "Our priority is to bring immediate relief to the people suffering and work toward a long-term peaceful resolution." ; "We are committed to merging the Luanda and Nairobi processes to create a more unified and effective approach," President Ruto added.

a66.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe (summit co-chair)
a66.speech: "We urge the government of the DRC to uphold the principles of peace and security by safeguarding diplomatic missions and ensuring the safety of all international personnel," Mnangagwa said.

a66.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe (summit co-chair)
a66.speech: "The sovereignty and territorial integrity of the DRC must be respected by all parties," said Mnangagwa.

a66.speaker: Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of Tanzania (summit host)
a66.speech: "We cannot allow this crisis to continue unchecked," said President Samia Suluhu Hassan of Tanzania, who hosted the summit. "We stand in solidarity with the people of DRC and will continue to support their efforts toward peace."

a153.speaker: “Seville Commitment”, UN declaration (document)
a153.speech: States that the aim is to “renew the global development financing framework”, at a moment of “serious geopolitical tensions and conflicts” and when the objectives agreed by the international community in the 2030 Agenda “are seriously behind schedule” ; “We are running out of time to reach our goals and to confront the adverse impacts of climate change. (...) The gap between our sustainable development aspirations and the financing to achieve them has continued to widen, particularly in developing countries, reaching an estimated value of 4 trillion dollars a year” ; across 68 pages it also emphasises that only the strengthening of multilateralism can respond to the urgent need to eradicate poverty and to confront the impacts of climate change, and recognises the sovereign debt of vulnerable and developing countries as one of the great obstacles to sustainable development.

a153.speaker: United Nations (calculations/data)
a153.speech: According to UN calculations, the current shortfall in development aid is 1.5 trillion more than ten years ago, and in 2024 official development assistance fell for the first time in six years, with a further 20% drop forecast for 2025.

a153.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a153.speech: Said recently that the Seville conference “is a unique opportunity to reform the international financial system”, which is today obsolete and dysfunctional.

a173.speaker: Dr Boa Jacques, maxillofacial surgeon at the Fada N'Gourma Regional Hospital Centre (CHR)
a173.speech: According to Dr Boa, a significant unmet need remains in the management of disfiguring pathologies, which are often neglected by traditional humanitarian aid; these conditions seriously compromise patients' social reintegration and psychological well-being, so it is essential to mobilise more resources and raise NGOs' awareness of this issue. The current security context constitutes a major obstacle to access to care; yet, with appropriate support, significant untapped potential remains to help a greater number of people.

a173.speaker: The patient's family
a173.speech: Deeply moved, expressed immense gratitude towards the entire care team.

a173.speaker: Centre Hospitalier Régional de Fada N'Gourma (source of the report)
a173.speech: Source: Fada N'Gourma Regional Hospital Centre, reporting the successful complex mandibular tumour removal and reconstruction carried out on 14 April 2025.

a579.speaker: US Embassy in Juba
a579.speech: Has reiterated its call on the transitional government to start using public revenue transparently to address the public needs.

a579.speaker: Michael J Adler, US Ambassador to South Sudan
a579.speech: Emphasized the need for South Sudan’s leaders to start demonstrating political will to put the interest of their people first; said the American people have long understood and supported the aspirations of the South Sudanese people for peace, freedom, and development; citing the nation’s $700 million in financial assistance over fiscal year 2023/2024 and more than $640 million in humanitarian assistance alone, said “South Sudanese people have the right to expect their government to take the steps necessary to reverse the longstanding trend of increased humanitarian need and to end aid dependency.” ; stated that the American people want to see the transitional government start taking the steps necessary to create an environment that is conducive to both effective development assistance and responsible private investment, including upholding human rights and holding those who violate these rights accountable ; “meeting peace commitments and creating conditions necessary to make the current extension of the transitional period the last one, ending with credible and peaceful elections without further delay” ; “these steps must include the transparent use of public revenue to appropriately pay for salaries, public services, humanitarian response, and other basic needs” ; said that the US government’s conviction is that the South Sudanese people should have a government that is accountable to them through elections and that uses public revenue appropriately and transparently; in his Tuesday’s concluding remark said that the time is long overdue for the South Sudanese people to enjoy the universal rights.

a709.speaker: Grace John Kenyi, Peace Activist and Human Rights Defender, speaking for a group of South Sudanese women activists
a709.speech: Emphasized the need for diplomatic missions to exert their influence in promoting peace and stability in South Sudan, saying that by leveraging diplomatic relations these missions can encourage actions that foster reconciliation and accountability; recognizing the humanitarian crisis, she emphasized the need for increased support for those impacted by the conflict. "We call upon diplomatic missions in South Sudan to use their diplomatic influence for peace in South Sudan, and encourage accountability and human rights, provide humanitarian assistance to those affected by the conflict," said Ms. Kenyi. ; "We urge collaborate with international partners to ensure lasting peace and stability through political and economic pressure on all the parties to the crisis."

a709.speaker: South Sudanese women activists (group)
a709.speech: Called for urgent local and international action to tackle ongoing political and security challenges in the country; they also appealed directly to the White Army and its leadership to embrace conflict resolution through peaceful means, expressing women's desire for a more constructive approach to resolving tensions.

a709.speaker: Michael Makuei, South Sudanese Information Minister
a709.speech: Termed the detention of some SPLM-IO politicians and commanders, including Petroleum Minister Puot Kang, Deputy Chief of Defense Force Duop Lam and an MP, as being in conflict with the law.

a709.speaker: Diplomatic missions from IGAD member states and Western governments
a709.speech: Have been calling for calm and restraint in South Sudan since the latest outbreak of large scale violence in Upper Nile, Western Equatoria and Western Bahr el Ghazal State.

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: In his 2023 inaugural lecture, described how for years he had successfully dodged requests to deliver the lecture by blaming the university's email system, and confessed he missed a trick during the Covid-19 pandemic, "when I could have done this online"; on being called by Standard Bank twice during the lecture: "I swear I turned this off …" ; on being interviewed: "I hate, hate, hate talking about myself."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On the ADVANCE trial results: the therapies worked but, as Venter puts it, "with complications peculiar to local populations, far from the sanitised world of curated pharmaceutical studies done on healthy white men."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: In a series of recent op-eds, has excoriated both the president and the health minister for providing scant leadership in the face of the US's defunding of the HIV response in South Africa, comparing their inaction to the infamous Aids denialism of former president Thabo Mbeki and his health minister Manto Tshabalala-Msimang.

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On being singled out: "There are so many people in the HIV world who did much more and more bravely."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On his childhood in Phalaborwa: "The town has a paint colour named after it — Phalaborwa Dust — a sort of dull grey, which says everything, really." ; "You couldn't have a family that size today." ; "They managed because the company subsidised everything from education to golf club memberships." ; "Growing up, I never met a black person who wasn't a servant." ; on school, that sadistic corporal punishment and other forms of bullying had become "entrenched to an unthinking level" ; "I worked like crazy at school, knowing that was my ticket out of there."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On Wits medical school under apartheid: "Instead, I walked into this amazing diversity of people. For a boy who grew up on Springbok Radio, it was more than I had dreamed of." ; "All the hospitals were segregated, our training was segregated, even blood was segregated — white patients would only be given blood from black donors in extreme cases. It was just insane."

a750.speaker: A lecturer friend of Venter (unnamed)
a750.speech: Calls Venter's way of speaking without any regard to self-preservation "borderline cancel language."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On student journalism and politics: "I enjoyed the cut and thrust of the media and understanding its place in political life"; credits journalism with making him a better HIV researcher and political organiser ("I was able to chair meetings and construct agendas. It helped me to write grants and manuscripts.") ; "The late 80s were some of the worst for apartheid repression. Fellow students were being detained and tortured, their families maimed and disappeared. There were these extreme ideologies on campus — the United Democratic Front was very active — but at the same time there were people in my class saying the activists had it coming. That dissonance was difficult, but as far as I was concerned, there was nowhere for a white person to hide, and joining the fight [against apartheid] was the only moral choice." ; maintains he was a "mediocre student, at odds with many of my classmates" ; "I found I was enjoying clinical medicine and realised I needed to really knuckle down in order to stay in it."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On apartheid healthcare and violence: "You go into the black hospitals and it's like, jeez, the things that are happening there. Meanwhile, white people are receiving world-class care." ; on the 1995 Yeoville stabbing: "It was 1995, and I was nearing the end of a year at Helen Joseph Hospital. In those days Rocky Street was still quite eclectic and happening and I was hanging out in a restaurant run by this Caribbean guy I knew. He had booted out a young drug addict, who went across the street and bought a knife, came back and stabbed him in the heart. It was 10am. I tried to resuscitate him, but I had nothing. The waiters continued to serve the customers and stuff, stepping over his body. It was just such a savage thing. He bled to death in front of me, and I was like, fuck South Africa and its trauma and violence." ; on his UK hospital job, which he found "terminally boring".

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On the peak of the HIV epidemic: "In some of the hospitals, like Bara [Baragwanath Hospital], you just left patients in casualty, and they would die there and go out the door. In Joburg Gen you put them on the floor in the corridors, and they died there waiting for a bed. It was brutal." ; cautions against apportioning blame: "The numbers had surged with a suddenness and severity that we still don't really understand. Nelson Mandela was trying to prevent a race war. There really wasn't much that he, or anybody else, could have done. I didn't understand the transmission enough and we didn't have the tools to prevent it." ; "As a junior doctor working in a Gauteng hospital I remember phoning the heads of health in the province and saying, 'We're full, can you redirect the ambulances?' As far as I could see there were people lying on the floor, largely dying of Aids, but also with strokes, heart attacks. They were dying of pneumonia and TB." ; "And looking back, that was the first sign of the absolute arrogance of some of the health people in government. And you see it now in the way foreigners and poor people are treated in the public sector. It is one thing to have no idea how to deal with a problem, but to lack the ability to do any reflection, have any empathy, and to self-correct is so upsetting."

a750.speaker: Gauteng provincial health administrator (unnamed, quoted by Venter)
a750.speech: "Who is from other provinces?" the administrator asked ; "Send them back." ; "I don't care, send them back, they're not supposed to be in Gauteng."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On discovering antiretroviral therapy: "The patient was one of a group that had HIV after receiving infected blood imported from the US by the state in the 1980s. The apartheid government took a decision to pay for their treatment with what was then extremely expensive antiretroviral therapy (ART), and the ANC government continued this." ; "I saw this patient in ICU just come off a ventilator, which just did not happen in those days." ; on Ian Sanne, who "taught me how to do clinical trials, how to play with these toxic, incredibly effective drugs, and it was really the first time I was able to start seeing myself as someone who was going to get involved in HIV. The drugs have evolved since then, now more effective with almost no side effects." ; "We were working from a hopelessly overcrowded outpatient clinic in the then Johannesburg Academic Hospital in which gay doctors had looked after gay men until the epidemic became more prevalent and they all left. I was working under this amazing endocrinologist called Jeffrey Wing and a dedicated Jewish GP called Clive Evian. At the time, it probably was the biggest HIV clinic on the continent, with queues out the door every day. That's where I learned about HIV outpatient medicine."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On NGOs, activists and the Treatment Action Campaign: "We needed each other. We needed access to the drugs and the Treatment Action Campaign had started smuggling them into the country. They needed proof that the drugs were effective in this context, and to treat their members and as many people as possible, and we had just started publishing findings from our cohort." ; "It was devastating, though, watching them fighting our government to even acknowledge HIV existed, while their members died needing those drugs. The hypocrisy of senior political figures, many of whom had family members on antiretrovirals I was treating, yet didn't call out Mbeki, is unforgivable."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On the medical profession's silence: "Other than the rural doctors, who have always fought for their patients, and the HIV Clinicians Society, the healthcare worker organisations were nowhere to be seen. The lawyers were there, civil society and the journalists, too, all fighting tooth and nail for access to therapy, but the professional organisations were too busy fighting for the interests of the profession." ; lamenting that little has changed: "Through Covid-19, and now with the defunding of HIV and scientific research, it is the same people raising their voices, and the same organisations sitting on their hands. Worryingly, a lot of the people we are fighting are the same ones who stood in the way of access during the Mbeki era."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On the Sleep Clinic and obesity clinic: "The quid pro quo is that they be allowed to advertise" ; "The new drugs for obesity are every bit as revolutionary as the HIV drugs, but every bit as fiddly as antiretrovirals were in 2000."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On donor dependency and the collapse of Pepfar and USAid: "It is nice not to have to worry about staff being pistol-whipped while at work" ; "What happened still feels quite unthinkable. On the one hand, it feels like 2004, when Mbeki's denial of HIV became national policy and everything felt like it was going backwards. On the other hand, it is extremely frustrating that our systems have not been made sustainable and are now on the brink of collapse as a result of Pepfar having been interwoven with the national HIV programme to such an extent everything unravels when it is stopped."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: Sketches a scenario in which South Africa's HIV response — "the one effective programme we have" — is misleadingly characterised as "too expensive" and dragged down to the lowest common denominator, "leading to the same terrible outcomes you find in crap programmes, like diabetes", with patients from neighbouring countries such as Lesotho crossing into South Africa en masse in search of treatment and being scapegoated by South African authorities. "A race to the bottom, in other words. We have poor indicators for almost every health metric outside of HIV, TB and vaccines, and even those are now slipping, due to the health department dropping the ball. Both our public and private health services are an expensive mess, for very different reasons. The health minister has been in charge for most of the last 17 years, we have endless excellent white papers and policy documents that gather dust, and little to show for the continent's most expensive health system."

a750.speaker: Francois Venter, Professor and head of Ezintsha, University of the Witwatersrand
a750.speech: On how to fix the health system: "It wasn't so long ago that we seemed to be in the grip of load-shedding without end, yet Eskom was turned around in 18 months. Our problems are systemic and we have enough resources and brains to fix them. What is needed is strong leadership, which is something we currently lack." ; "I'll tell you what you do. You take the top people from the medical aids and tell them: 'You can't be head of Discovery or the Government Employee Medical Scheme, Gems, anymore, lead with the best people from academia, from government, the private sector, donors, civil society, form a focused group with teeth, and run the health system.'" ; "We all declare our interests, put an end to corruption, and everyone from the president and the minister of health down in government must use the public healthcare system when using their medical aid. If they experience the system first hand, they will have an immediate investment in assisting those fixing it. Stop blaming the private sector and a lack of money for the problem." ; "Start using the innovations South Africans are world leaders in, including data systems. If we do that, I am telling you, we will fix the system in five years."

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: "Order has been restored" ; "For people like me who relied on live shows, concerts, and such, we were affected by Covid-19 and it feels good to be back in front of a live audience, doing what I love. I am home, but I am still very much a New York girl. I will be going back in a couple of days."

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: "I was working. People tend to think that when they don't see what it is that you are doing, you are not busy, but I have many surprises on the pipeline." ; "The US is tough. It needs you to know your story. People have been wondering what it is I'm doing in New York, and I have been hush-hush about it, but when the material drop, people will be pleasantly surprised" ; "New York is tough. It is cut-throat and lonely, but I love the challenge. The US is massive, and everyone is trying to make it. They are also the crème de la crème of entertainment, they created it. It's the heaven of showbiz. I did not get there and become the Bonang that is known in my country and continent. I needed to work to prove myself all the way to the top. The experience has been different in many ways."

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: On her business ventures and her Méthode Cap Classique brand, House of BNG: "I had to tackle the US as a wine expert for my brand BNG and meet incredible investors. But I also had to look at it from a personality perspective, to see. Africa is the trend right now, everyone is looking to us for music and fashion." ; "Every year, we like to bring a new flavour to the people who have supported us. The timing needed to be perfect because I do things with intention and choose the projects that I do carefully. I like to be associated with things that make sense. I am also announcing another project very soon." ; "I relied on selling my MCC. I have been working since the age of 16 and never paused. I don't take anyone and anything for granted, which has given me longevity. Kuli Roberts taught me how to speak to journalists and the media and that made me who I am. People at home make me famous in New York."

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: On her legal dispute with management agency CSA Global, which she announced in October 2021 she had terminated her contract with, taking legal action and investigating possible criminal conduct: "There was and still is a huge legal battle around BNG that is still ongoing. I can't say too much because the matter is sub judice. But BNG is here, doing well. It is my brand; my heart and soul and we are launching something major. There will come a time when I will explain what exactly happened to me and people need to learn from it. It's a lesson I learned and it's a mistake that anyone can make and because we trust people, we end up in complicated situations" ; "Which is why I am so grateful for Covid-19. It made me stop and see people for who they are. Had there not been a pandemic, I would not have stopped to see what was happening, so I am grateful for the lessons. When I eventually say, people will be surprised."

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: On her career ambitions abroad: "It has been good to me. It's something I've always wanted to do, since a young girl, I knew that I would start at home and then work towards being international." ; "I always wanted to challenge myself when I felt I had reached the roof at home. I wanted to see what was out there. In terms of business and live productions, it doesn't get bigger than the Miss SA pageant, SAMAs, Metros, and the Sports Awards which I have all done and there isn't anything left for me to do, and the next step was to either go international or remain in the same place without growth. The next step was for me to see the world and where I can go."

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: On life in New York: "It's not all glitz and glam. New York has a lot of people but is one of the loneliest places in the world. If you're going to attack it alone, you will have moments of self-doubt. I am lucky because I have some family in the US but I went there on my own and with my assistant. It is a very lonely and tough place at times, I don't know many people. But I am making new friends and building. I also wanted to live like that, go out, sit at the park, be anonymous and do things that I wouldn't be able to do be home without being noticed. But of course, there are a few people who will know who I am but it's great to walk around and not have everyone recognize you. That's the life I wanted."

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: On home and Nigeria: "I love how people appreciate me at home. I have never let fame get to my head. I have remained real and who I am and that is what people love about me, even when I am away with no shows or red carpets to host." ; "I think Lagos is an incredible city with amazing people. The nightlife and the glam teams are superb, and I resonate with the high level of excellence there. It reminds me a lot of New York City. Nigerians expect a lot from each other, high delivery, black excellence and I resonate with that because they want to be the best. They inspire me and we can really take a lot from them." ; "We have some amazing and unique things about us that make us stand out and home will always be close to my heart. It birthed me into my brand and the person I am today."

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: On her relationship: "I have been dating my American guy for about a year and four months now" ; "But I just feel, the last time I introduced someone to my fans and followers, things just went pear-shaped. Showing my relationships has never benefited me in any way. It has brought me worse than good, and I learned that the hard way. I feel like I make more money when people don't know who I am dating. But I am happy in this relationship. You can see my happiness in my glow and ake shoti ka nex." ; "Just because it's not on Instagram, doesn't mean it's not happened. My fans don't love it when I keep secrets, but I have been burned in the past and I am being careful."

a803.speaker: A Twitter influencer (unnamed)
a803.speech: Alleged that Bonang Matheba had done some surgery on her nose.

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: Responded to the allegation by saying, "I'm all for entertainment journalism, just don't ruin the fun for everyone. It's weird" ; "Argh, I was not offended by the nose comment. I understand what entertainment all is about and I know what to take seriously and what not. People think I had work done on my nose but there is make-up contouring and filters" ; "I have had worse things said about me and buying a nose is the least of my worries. I know how to handle critics."

a803.speaker: Bonang Matheba, South African media personality
a803.speech: On how her goals have changed: "My goals have changed with time, mostly after launching BNG. I did not expect it to grow and be as big as it is now. It is the number one selling MCC at Woolworths and it has changed my life and showed me another dimension to the business" ; "I was always a TV and radio girl but because of the success of my wine, I've had to make a huge change. It takes a lot of my time, and it is my heart and soul."

a1019.speaker: Alain Tribert Mutabazi, Minister of National Defence and Veterans Affairs of Burundi
a1019.speech: Called on the population of Rumonge province to take ownership of the Burundian government's Vision 2040-2060 and to embrace all sectors of national life; in his greeting speech said that they took part in these community development works in the province because peace and security reign there as well as throughout the national territory: "We must take advantage of this situation to devote ourselves to income-generating activities."

a1019.speaker: Alain Tribert Mutabazi, Minister of National Defence and Veterans Affairs of Burundi
a1019.speech: After conveying the greetings of the Burundian head of state to the people of Rumonge, praised the pace of development of Rumonge province, noting that it will contribute significantly to achieving Burundi's Vision of an emerging country by 2040 and a developed country by 2060 ; "Natives of Rumonge living abroad have the good practice of contributing to the sustainable development of their home province. This should serve as a model for other members of the Diaspora in order to build our country"; also called on them to always take part in community development works and to obey the authorities.

a1019.speaker: Alain Tribert Mutabazi, Minister of National Defence and Veterans Affairs of Burundi
a1019.speech: Indicated that families and the local administration must take ownership of the question of children's education, in order to promote inclusive education to support Burundi's vision, and stressed that the construction and equipping of schools must be a priority because education is the pillar of sustainable development.

a1019.speaker: Alain Tribert Mutabazi, Minister of National Defence and Veterans Affairs of Burundi
a1019.speech: Said the province offers many opportunities that can contribute to sustainable development: specified that industrial fishing on Lake Tanganyika should be promoted to increase export products and bring in the foreign currency the country badly needs, and insisted that the exploitation of agricultural land is of great importance to increase production and fight famine within families.

a1019.speaker: Alain Tribert Mutabazi, Minister of National Defence and Veterans Affairs of Burundi
a1019.speech: With Burundi approaching elections, made a strong appeal to the population of Rumonge never to listen to ill-intentioned people carrying divisive, false or hateful messages: "The Burundian head of state, Evariste Ndayishimiye, has given us, as father of the nation, a guideline to follow to build the country and contribute to development. And in the coming elections, we are all called upon to choose leaders who will back and support the Burundian head of state in achieving the 2040-2060 vision"; gave assurances that the Burundian government will spare no effort to put in place initiatives and programmes that can contribute to the well-being of the Burundian people.

a1093.speaker: Digeo Kahlari, Namibian swimming coach and owner of Infinity Swimming Club
a1093.speech: Says his recent trip to the United States for the American Swimming Coaches Association (ASCA) world clinic has given him invaluable lessons that he wants to impart to the local swimming community, and described the journey as long but rewarding ; "It took four flights to get there, but it was worthwhile. To see African coaches in attendance was a proud moment, and it also gave us an opportunity to network."

a1093.speaker: Digeo Kahlari, Namibian swimming coach and owner of Infinity Swimming Club
a1093.speech: "The road for swimming is becoming narrow because of technology that is constantly changing. You might think you are doing the right thing, but it could be outdated already. That is why it's so important for coaches to constantly equip themselves with the latest knowledge and tools." ; mentioned innovations such as the "endless pool", where swimmers train while being monitored through video analysis ; "America is the leading swimming country in the world, and the way they use technology in training is amazing. It shows us how far we still have to go."

a1093.speaker: Digeo Kahlari, Namibian swimming coach and owner of Infinity Swimming Club
a1093.speech: Stressed that Namibia must invest in both swimmers and equipment if the country hopes to catch up with global standards ; "I learnt that there are more than 300 000 active swimmers in the USA, which shows how big their pool of talent is. We need to start investing in our own athletes and coaches to close that gap."

a1093.speaker: Digeo Kahlari, Namibian swimming coach and owner of Infinity Swimming Club
a1093.speech: "The work starts now. My biggest goal is not only to apply these methods here, but also to take our swimmers to international meets in the US so they can get accustomed to competing at that level. At home, you might think your swimmers are good, but once they compete abroad, you see the difference."

a1196.speaker: UNAIDS
a1196.speech: said that at least one status report on the impact of cuts has been received from 55 different countries up to the start of this week. That includes 42 projects that are supported by the US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and 13 that receive some US support.

a1196.speaker: UNAIDS
a1196.speech: reported just over a week later that there was widespread "confusion" over how the waiver was being implemented on the ground.

a1196.speaker: UNAIDS country office reports (16 reports, week of 17-21 February)
a1196.speech: show that these waivers have led to the resumption of some clinical services, such as HIV treatment and prevention of vertical transmission, in many countries that are highly dependent on US funding.

a1196.speaker: UNAIDS (UN agency)
a1196.speech: said it's unclear how long funding will last amid multiple reports that key US government systems and staff responsible for paying implementing partners are either offline or working at greatly reduced capacity; and that critical layers of national AIDS responses are ineligible for these waivers, including many HIV prevention and community-led services for key populations and adolescent girls and young women. Data collection and analysis services have been disrupted in numerous countries, and the overall quantity and quality of HIV prevention, testing and treatment services has been eroded. Staff working in health facilities are facing increased workloads, and patients are experiencing increased wait times to receive lifesaving services.

a1196.speaker: UNAIDS situation report
a1196.speech: "US Government statements to UN system organizations suggest US-funded programmes focused on gender equality and transgender populations may not resume," according to the UNAIDS situation report. The situation report covers more granular analysis on the global AIDS response's heavy reliance on US foreign assistance, extracted from the datasets managed by UNAIDS... The report also named the 20 countries that rely most heavily on funding from Washington: DRC, Haiti, Mozambique, Tanzania, Zambia, Uganda, Nigeria, Rwanda, Angola, Kenya, Ukraine, Burkina Faso, Burundi, El Salvador, Zimbabwe, Togo, Nepal, Côte d'Ivoire, Eswatini and Benin.

a1196.speaker: Global HIV Prevention Coalition (estimates)
a1196.speech: Before the freeze, the US Government provided two thirds of international financing for HIV prevention in low and middle-income countries, according to estimates from the Global HIV Prevention Coalition.

a1196.speaker: US Government statements to UN system organizations
a1196.speech: suggest US-funded programmes focused on gender equality and transgender populations may not resume.

a1196.speaker: UNAIDS (UN agency)
a1196.speech: said civil society and community-led interventions are central to ending AIDS and to sustaining the gains into the future, and that people living with HIV and key populations at higher risk of infection play a crucial role in maintaining the local services needed to stay healthy.

a1701.speaker: Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition of Mali (Army General), speaking through his Prime Minister, General Abdoulaye Maïga
a1701.speech: Declared that this collapse, which is not the first of its kind, will not go unpunished.

a1701.speaker: Douga Kéita, chief of the village of Bilaly Koto (his words reported by his son Tiémoko Keita)
a1701.speech: Held that the ministerial delegation minimised the gravity of this tragedy and the danger that Chinese gold-panning sites represent for the population and the environment in general: "What happened in my village is more than a devastating tragedy. I have always denounced the presence of the Chinese in gold panning, because they respect no rules. I personally told the Ministers of Mines and of the Environment and Sanitation that the presence of the Chinese constitutes a real danger for the whole commune. I also told them that I no longer wanted a Chinese presence in my village and that they should do everything to make them leave. But the ministers curtly replied that they did not have that power. That is when I realised that the ministerial delegation had not grasped the extent of the gravity of the situation."

a1701.speaker: Abdoulaye Touré, vice-president of the local Federation of Gold Panners of the Kéniéba cercle
a1701.speech: "The Federation, as its name indicates, aims to manage the mining sector at the local level and to ensure that gold can shine for Kéniéba and for Mali as a whole. It is also about reorganising the mining sector, notably gold panning. To that end, we began to register all the gold-panning sites of the Kéniéba cercle with the support of a bailiff. In a word, we wanted to clean up the gold-panning sector and put an end to the many collapses that the cercle continues to experience. But to our great surprise, the Directorate General of Territorial Administration decided to suspend all our activities."

a1701.speaker: Directorate General of Territorial Administration (confidential letter dated 6 November 2024)
a1701.speech: Suspended the Federation's activities on the grounds that it had substituted itself for the recognised actors in the mining sector and was engaging in racketeering.

a1701.speaker: Officials of the local Federation of Gold Panners of the Kéniéba cercle
a1701.speech: Categorically reject these accusations, challenging the said letter before the courts.

a1701.speaker: Adama Foulo Sissoko, member of the local Federation of Gold Panners of the Kéniéba cercle
a1701.speech: "All our problems began when we introduced a system for registering gold-panning sites. Because when a gold-panning site was to open, the customary chiefs collected two million every month as a land right. The former bureau of the Federation also received millions per month. But with the registration system we have put in place, everything is clear and traceable. Everyone knows what has been paid during the month and the year, and it goes directly into the treasury. For us, this system is truly transparent. The main actors in the racketeering are known to everyone, including the State. It is the former president of the Chamber of Mines of Kéniéba, Lassane Camara, who orchestrated all this so that our Federation would be suspended, because he does not want transparency in the management of gold panning. All our activities are blocked by this measure. We are asking for this measure to be lifted so that we can continue our activities."

a1701.speaker: Another official of the local Federation of Gold Panners
a1701.speech: "Our adversaries went and said that we carried out illegal registrations in their communes without a mandate, which is false. Before the judge, we presented all our legal documents, which convinced the judge to release us. We want the well-being of the gold panners of Kéniéba and also a fair redistribution of gold-panning revenues among all the sons and daughters of Kéniéba. If you see that collapses are multiplying, it is because the resources are badly managed. It is only a handful of people who benefit from what is owed to a whole village or commune. We are asking the directorate of territorial administration to review its decision."

a1701.speaker: A young man from Sitakily (anonymous)
a1701.speech: "If we see that Chinese gold panning has taken on an unprecedented scale to the point that no one can do anything, it is because of the involvement of young people. Because it is young people who are the focal point of these Chinese wherever they go. Moreover, the young people are strongly supported by civil society and the former bureau of the Federation. The worst of it all is that you do not even dare file a complaint against them for violating the environment and the ecosystem with the abusive use of cyanide. They are also supported by the local administrative authorities, first of all the prefect and the gendarmerie."

a1701.speaker: Environmentalists
a1701.speech: Are categorical: the use of cyanide carries significant risks, notably the contamination of soils and watercourses, as well as dangers for workers and surrounding communities.

a1701.speaker: A resident of Bilaly Koto (anonymous)
a1701.speech: "The Chinese respect nothing in terms of protecting the environment. Because of the use of cyanide, we lack drinking water in the village and a pond where our children bathe. Without their parents' knowledge, it is in these highly toxic waters that the children bathe. As a result, the children very quickly catch cardiovascular diseases and skin burns. We have lost many children because of this. Less than a week ago, I lost about ten head of livestock that had drunk water contaminated with cyanide, because we do everything to keep the animals away from these waters."

a1701.speaker: Another resident of Kéniéba town (anonymous), whose house is 100 metres from an open-pit gold-panning site abandoned by the Chinese
a1701.speech: "AngloGold Ashanti Mali, Barrick Gold Mali Ltd, Avnel Gold, Chaka Mining, Loulo and Consolidated Mining Corporation, all these companies use cyanide with extreme caution. They follow strict safety protocols to minimise the risks. But the Chinese and the Burkinabè respect absolutely nothing. We no longer have land on which we can farm, no more flora and fauna because of these Chinese and Burkinabè."

a1701.speaker: The local Federation of Gold Panners of the Kéniéba cercle
a1701.speech: Calls for a reorganisation of gold panning so that the gold shines first for the people of Kéniéba and so that everyone benefits in terms of economic returns for Kéniéba and for Mali in general.

a1701.speaker: An official of the local Federation of Gold Panners (anonymous)
a1701.speech: "To reorganise the gold-panning sector, the government need only entrust this task to the local Federation of Gold Panners of Kéniéba. Because we know this sector and we live in it. We are not against exploitation by the Chinese and the Burkinabè. But this exploitation must be accompanied by support measures. For example, if a Chinese person comes with his exploitation permit, a fund must be set aside for securing the site and, after exploitation, for the rehabilitation of the site."

a1701.speaker: An official of the local Federation of Gold Panners (anonymous)
a1701.speech: "Since last September, we have drawn up a memorandum built around seven strategic axes. By carefully exploiting these axes, the reorganisation of the gold-panning sector will be very simple for those who know the sector. On Wednesday 26 February 2025, the proposals adopted in the council of ministers to reorganise the sector were drawn from the memorandum we presented during our meeting with the former Prime Minister Choguel Maïga. To avoid collapses, we have adopted a policy consisting of setting aside more than 20 shovels of banco. The women take this banco and wash it. With this policy, you will see that exploitation will continue, the women will not go down into the site and no one will die. As for security, we will place members of the Federation around the site to avoid disorder. First of all, those who have their exploitation permit will dig a basin where the dirty water will be stored and, after exploitation, we will close the site in order to rehabilitate it." ; He remains convinced that if the government applies the said memorandum to the letter, the gold-panning sector would be well organised and would generate for the State alone more than 10 billion CFA francs per quarter: "If we manage to properly reorganise gold panning, which is largely dominated by the Chinese, I assure you that we could collect more than 10 billion CFA francs per quarter. But one only needs to know the sector and its ins and outs for Kéniéba and Mali as a whole to benefit from the economic returns. Imagine: in three months we have more than 10 billion, but in one year Kéniéba alone can generate more than 300 billion CFA francs for the State. These resources generated by gold panning could allow the State to finance development projects and to pay all of Mali's civil servants. But in this cacophony, it is first of all Kéniéba that has lost out, given that we already have no road, no hospitals, still less drinking water."

a1883.speaker: US Agency for International Development (USAID) (official statement)
a1883.speech: said thousands of employees will be placed on leave from Friday night; the order would affect all "direct-hire personnel" except those on "mission-critical functions, core leadership and specially designated programs", and employees would be notified by Thursday afternoon; in a statement on its website on Tuesday USAID said it would work with the US Department of State to arrange and pay for return travel for personnel posted outside the US within 30 days, and that employees who are part of the exceptions would be told by 15:00 EDT on Thursday. The statement concluded with the message: "Thank you for your service."

a1883.speaker: Trump administration
a1883.speech: has said USAID is wasting money and needs to align with the president's policy priorities.

a1883.speaker: USAID agency staff, backed by Democratic lawmakers
a1883.speech: have protested over the cuts, saying they will put lives in danger and hamper national security.

a1883.speaker: Congressional Research Service (data cited)
a1883.speech: According to the Congressional Research Service, the agency employs 10,000 people worldwide and two-thirds of those people work overseas.

a1883.speaker: Official figures (cited)
a1883.speech: USAID, founded in 1961, has a budget of around $40bn (£32.25bn) per year, amounting to roughly 0.6% of federal spending, according to official figures.

a1883.speaker: United Nations
a1883.speech: said Tuesday that it had been notified by the US that it was freezing $13.3m in aid destined for Haiti.

a1883.speaker: US State Department
a1883.speech: issued a waiver on Wednesday exempting $40.7m of foreign assistance for Haiti's national police and the UN-backed international security support mission.

a1883.speaker: White House (statement)
a1883.speech: put out a statement listing a number of projects that it called evidence of "waste and abuse", including a grant of $1.5m to an LGBTQ group in Serbia and $2.5m for electric vehicles in Vietnam.

a1883.speaker: USAID email to staff (document obtained by BBC News)
a1883.speech: told employees they had been placed on paid administrative leave and must remain "available" by telephone and email during business hours, but were not allowed to enter USAID buildings.

a1883.speaker: Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX
a1883.speech: has suggested USAID should be shut down entirely, as it is "beyond repair".

a1883.speaker: HIV patient in Nigeria (anonymous)
a1883.speech: told the BBC that she and others are worried that free anti-retroviral drugs, funded by USAID, would be cut off: "I am really scared about what the future holds given all that is going on in America. I got my last set of HIV drugs in November and I am supposed to go back in April... but I don't know what would happen by then." ; "These free drugs are really important for me and most of us (HIV patients) would be in trouble if it is affected."

a1883.speaker: Democrats in Washington DC
a1883.speech: have been particularly critical of changes to the agency, calling them "illegal" and "unconstitutional".

a1883.speaker: Andy Kim, New Jersey Democratic Senator
a1883.speech: wrote on social media: "[USAID is] a foreign policy tool with bipartisan origins that is critical in this dangerous global environment." ; "Gutting it means gutting our ability to compete and keep America safe."

a2030.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB), 2021 Annual Development Effectiveness Review
a2030.speech: Tracks the Bank's activities along the High 5s, the main programme areas that focus on improving access to energy, addressing food insecurity, industrialisation, continental economic integration and improving the standard of living of Africans; the Review paints a rather positive outlook of resilience despite the public health and economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic.

a2030.speaker: Abdul Kamara (PhD), AfDB East Africa deputy director-general
a2030.speech: On the pandemic's impact and the Bank's response: "The pandemic, when it hit, nobody would have thought we would still be grappling with it. It affected the way we work, the way we deliver and how we measure results. It also affected our programmes because countries had to grapple with increased expenditure to boost their health systems to respond to the crisis and at the same time revenues were going down because of COVID-related travel restrictions and lockdowns. Economic activity went down. We had to come in and we came in a very big way. We launched a three billion dollar bond in the financial markets in 2020. We came in handy to help countries scale up social support systems but also on being economically resilient. This applies to Ethiopia as well. For example, we approved grants and positioned the country to scale up its rural and urban safety net programme and helped the government to bump up liquidity through banks. We did similar things for other countries."

a2030.speaker: Abdul Kamara (PhD), AfDB East Africa deputy director-general
a2030.speech: On the long-term impacts of the crisis: "It has the potential to roll back economic gains that we have made over the last decade. Africa was on a very positive trajectory but in 2020 it recorded a contraction of 1.8pc in GDP. Going forward, we need to focus on healthcare infrastructure and education. We do not want ever again to be caught unawares as we did, where things like personal protective gear had to come from overseas. We will support healthcare policy going forward, building diagnostic and pharmaceutical capacity and R&D." ; "The slowness to accessing vaccines poses a risk. There is no country in Africa that has reached the targeted level of vaccination for herd immunity to be established. The potential is there. We are in dialogue with countries such as South Africa, Senegal and Morocco to develop the capacity to manufacture vaccines." ; said healthcare infrastructure also means access to power and technology, pointing to the High 5s — Power Africa, Feed Africa, the Seqota grant in Ethiopia where half of all children under five are affected by stunting, and support for integrated agro-industrial parks.

a2030.speaker: Abdul Kamara (PhD), AfDB East Africa deputy director-general
a2030.speech: On why AfDB ranks high on quality of development assistance: "This is because of our well-balanced investments and understanding the needs of African countries. When the pandemic hit, we focused on resources, on the way we deliver and the differences we make in people's lives. It is an approach that gives emphasis to dialogue and economic analysis. It informs our country strategy paper." ; "We also make sure that our support is aligned with the country's priority... Over 60pc of our investment has been in infrastructure – power, roads and sanitation. There is the Mombasa-Nairobi-Addis Abeba road, and the Ethiopia-Kenya electricity transmission line. There is the connection between Ethiopia and Djibouti, which is a very important corridor for this continent." ; "It is important for us that countries take ownership of our work with them... We look at environmental issues and have a very thorough vetting process. Is a road we are building going to pass through people's homes, are they being compensated and informed?"

a2030.speaker: Abdul Kamara (PhD), AfDB East Africa deputy director-general
a2030.speech: On political uncertainty, conflict and development: "Development plays a crucial role in peace and stability. It goes two ways. When conflict arises, you need a political solution. But we also recognise the role of development assistance in terms of addressing poverty, inequality and bringing connectivity so that some regions are not marginalised." ; cited the Four Towns water project in Ethiopia, the Gibe hydroelectric power projects and the Addis Abeba transmission and distribution network project with JICA ; "On top of this, in the post-conflict time, development support helps consolidate peace. In this, we have at the AfDB the Transition Support Facility. It does a very thorough analysis of every country. It identifies the drivers of fragility upfront, including lack of development opportunities. It also looks at levers of change to make sure that growth is inclusive."

a2030.speaker: Abdul Kamara (PhD), AfDB East Africa deputy director-general
a2030.speech: On the African Continental Free Trade Area: "We commend African governments for taking such broad initiatives. We are supporting the African Union on the Trade Area. The positivity around it is fully justified. It can be a game-changer that will address the problems of Africa's small and fragmented markets by creating a single market. It will boost trade, improve the competitiveness of the continent and enhance the attractiveness of the continent as an investment destination." ; "It will be easier said than done though. There are pre-requisites with legislations and regulations. Primarily, the internal productivity constraints of countries have to be addressed. You cannot have a free market if you are not producing, if you are only importing or are not adding value. Infrastructure is key here."

a2030.speaker: Abdul Kamara (PhD), AfDB East Africa deputy director-general
a2030.speech: On the transition to renewable energy: "All developed economies have benefited from cheap sources of energy. And Africa is rich in fossil fuel reserves. Countries like Nigeria, Algeria and Angola are dependent on oil production. They should be granted the opportunity to industrialise and trade with the rest of the continent, and support continent-wide industrialisation." ; "That said, governments and development partners need to focus on the transition to renewables and cleaner energy, and over time transition away from non-renewables. But we have to ensure it does not cause revenue and job losses. The transition has to be managed justly to not affect Africa's industrialisation and economic development." ; "We are committed to ceasing investment in coal and oil exploration in the long-term, in a phased manner."

a2030.speaker: Abdul Kamara (PhD), AfDB East Africa deputy director-general
a2030.speech: On optimism for the continent: "We are very optimistic as we have to appreciate how far the continent has come. For instance, Africa's resilience during the COVID-19 crisis goes a long way to send the message that it is not necessarily as fragile as the world has been made to believe." ; "There is a caveat with climate change. Although Africa contributes least to global warming, it's worst hit by its impacts. There is a risk there. But dialogue is going on at very high levels. Many commitments have been made during the COP26. Our leaders are also becoming vocal in articulating their position and in showing that those who are polluting more take responsibility to help us in adaptation." ; "Taking all of this, I have every reason to be optimistic. There are challenges, including conflict, but that is part of life. But the recognition now is that we are capable of addressing them and that they would not derail or remove us from our development trajectory."

a2399.speaker: Fin24 (report)
a2399.speech: Recently reported that greylisting is expected to hike the cost of doing business in South Africa by increasing the amount of due diligence companies have to carry out, and that South Africans may also find sending funds offshore and transacting with international banks more difficult. “The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) decision to put South Africa on the grey list signals to global banks, financial institutions and investors that the country is not fully compliant with anti-money laundering and terrorist financing standards.” The move puts South Africa in the company of countries such as Syria, Haiti, Yemen and Mozambique, Fin24 reported.

a2399.speaker: Bank of Namibia
a2399.speech: Noted that Namibia is going to great lengths to meet the deadlines in order to avoid the country from being greylisted after the current 12-month monitoring period expires; if the country is greylisted, the FATF will closely monitor the country’s financial transactions with the rest of the world, and the country’s financial system may suffer reputational damage, affecting foreign direct investment, capital flows, and increasing compliance costs.

a2399.speaker: Johannes !Gawaxab, Bank of Namibia Governor
a2399.speech: “Notwithstanding these recent developments in our region, we have seen countries close to home successfully exiting the heightened surveillance through resolute commitment and action from all stakeholders. Namibia is better positioned to safeguard its interests and protect its financial system because of the demonstrable political will and widespread support from all stakeholders. We are encouraged that investors regard Namibia as a safe investment destination, and the enforceability of our legal framework is undeniable, thanks to our strong institutions and independent judiciary. We reassure Namibians and our valued stakeholders all over the world of our commitment to fight financial crimes and, that our financial system is robust and will be in better shape at the end of these interventions.”

a2399.speaker: Josef Sheehama, economic analyst
a2399.speech: According to him, the Namibian economy is closely linked to South Africa, with the Namibian dollar pegged one-to-one to the South African Rand, and a currency peg is dangerous for it can produce the wrong political and economic implications; greylisting may hinder Namibian economic growth and development, and global correspondent banks are likely to demand a higher level of due diligence. “This will affect crossborder capital flows, especially for the trade sector. Documentary requirements for export and import payments, such as letters of credit, may become more challenging to fulfil, potentially raising costs and hampering business for companies engaged in trade. These changes will make Namibia and South Africa’s foreign-exchange control regime more restrictive, although we do not expect this to create any major barriers to ongoing trade and investment flows for the economy as a whole.” ; “It is important to take note that what is good for South Africa is good for Namibia. It is unfortunate that greylisting by FAFT will directly or indirect affect us due to the currency peg.”

a2405.speaker: Ousman Surur, Director of the Federal Cooperative Agency
a2405.speech: “The blending factories are meant to increase the production and productivity of the farmers in the country through the supply of appropriate fertilizer to the soils.” ; “The blending factory quit producing as the result of unspecified fertilizers purchased as an input.”

a2405.speaker: Agricultural Transformation Agency (ATA) 2013/14 report
a2405.speech: Indicated that sulfur, potassium, boron and zinc nutrients are deficient in many areas, so that one compound fertilizer NPS and five blended fertilizers – NPSB, NPKSB, NPSZnB, NPKSZnB, and NPSZn – are needed to address the key nutrient deficiencies in the tested soils.

a2405.speaker: Federal Cooperative Agency
a2405.speech: According to the agency, Gibe Dedessa and Becho Weliso Farmers’ Cooperative Union in Oromia Regional state registered success at least in small scale for the first batch of production ; according to the Agency, the government is to pay nearly 252.7 million birr to the cooperatives based on the report of the Auditor General.

a2405.speaker: Auditor General (report)
a2405.speech: Cited as the basis on which the government is to pay nearly 252.7 million birr to the cooperative unions.

a2617.speaker: Ryan Cooper, editor-in-chief of The American Prospect
a2617.speech: “We should not underestimate the destructive power of stupidity,” writes Ryan Cooper in The American Prospect, in the article ‘Musk and Trump are causing the dumbest imperial collapse in history’. “USAID,” he stresses, “the world’s largest distributor of humanitarian aid, did a tremendous job — until now. The agency has been almost dismantled, unleashing havoc across the globe. HIV and drug-resistant tuberculosis are now spreading uncontrolled in many countries that depend on USAID medication, proving that the United States is not reliable and threatening outbreaks of these diseases in the United States itself.”

a2617.speaker: Financial Times survey
a2617.speech: Reveals that more than 60% of Americans believe US foreign aid is wasted “on corruption or administrative fees”; the survey highlights widespread public dissatisfaction with the way foreign aid is allocated and administered.

a2617.speaker: Elon Musk, head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a2617.speech: Announced on 3 February that, together with President Donald Trump, they would restructure USAID; a critic of USAID on X (formerly Twitter), he accused the agency of “funding the DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion] agenda abroad while America goes bankrupt at home”.

a2617.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2617.speech: Signed an executive order to halt foreign aid funding as soon as he took office; the measure provoked a reaction from many Democrats, although some expressed support for reducing foreign aid spending.

a2617.speaker: US Congress (data)
a2617.speech: According to Congress, USAID allocated more than 40 billion dollars in foreign aid during fiscal year 2023.

a2617.speaker: CNN
a2617.speech: Has explained that Elon Musk is misleading Americans about government spending.

a2617.speaker: Elon Musk, head of DOGE
a2617.speech: When questioned about inaccurate statements, admitted that “some of the things I say will be incorrect and should be corrected”; he also shared a post by an X user claiming that “USAID spent taxpayer money to fund celebrity trips to Ukraine, all to boost Zelensky’s popularity among Americans” — a post including a video made to look like it came from the entertainment channel E! News, which was a fabrication; he criticised the US for supposedly sending 50 million dollars in condoms to Mozambique — which also never happened.

a2617.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House press secretary
a2617.speech: Announced at her first White House press conference that the Trump administration had detected and thwarted a planned expenditure of 50 million dollars “to fund condoms in Gaza”, attributing the alleged discovery in part to Musk’s DOGE team.

a2617.speaker: Elon Musk, head of DOGE
a2617.speech: Promoted Leavitt’s words on X, writing that it was the “tip of the iceberg” and that “a lot of that money ended up in the pockets [of] Hamas, not actually in condoms” — a claim that was pure nonsense, and for which the White House never had any proof.

a2617.speaker: Mia Malan, editor of the health journalism site Bhekisisa
a2617.speech: Told NPR: “Although the South African government pays for most of the country’s antiretroviral medicines, it receives significant help from non-profit organisations, which are funded by the US government, to supply health professionals to public-sector clinics” ; “There is no point having all those pills if we cannot get them to the people who need them. And for that we need health professionals.”

a2617.speaker: Study revealed by the newspaper Público
a2617.speech: Shows that the Portuguese consider helping poorer countries important, but the majority want something in return; compared with a similar study in 2006, whereas before only a minimal percentage (2.1%) considered that too much was spent on cooperation, that figure has now risen to 32.4%, and whereas almost 17 years ago half of respondents (50.3%) were of the opinion that Portugal did not invest sufficient resources in that area, today that opinion is held by a minority (7.3%); in 2006, 74% agreed that development cooperation should be done without conditions, while today only 45% believe one should give without asking anything in return.

a2617.speaker: Instituto Camões (official development assistance data)
a2617.speech: Data published by the Instituto Camões show that in 2023 – the latest figures available – Cabo Verde was the fourth country that received the most gross ODA (16 million 547 thousand euros), behind Mozambique, Angola and São Tomé and Príncipe, out of a total envelope of more than 177 million euros for the PALOP countries and Timor-Leste.

a2691.speaker: U.S. officials
a2691.speech: Upon review, U.S. officials determined that the [$850,000 USAID Somalia] contract lacked tangible deliverables or measurable impact aligned with American strategic interests or the public good.

a2691.speaker: U.S. officials (on scope of the review)
a2691.speech: Officials emphasized that this is only the beginning of a larger effort to increase financial oversight and strengthen efficiency across government operations.

a2691.speaker: Spokesperson for the federal oversight team (anonymous)
a2691.speech: Stated, "We are committed to ensuring that every dollar of taxpayer money is used wisely. This ongoing review process will help us redirect resources toward programs with clear, measurable outcomes that serve the American people and our strategic interests abroad.”

a2703.speaker: World Bank
a2703.speech: Predicts that Sub-Saharan Africa will be home to most of the world's poor by 2030.

a2767.speaker: Disaster Management Agency (DMA), Somalia
a2767.speech: Has reported that approximately 6 million people, including entire families, are at risk of famine unless immediate humanitarian assistance is provided.

a2767.speaker: Displaced families in Mogadishu
a2767.speech: Have claimed that the aid intended for them is frequently stolen, leaving them to fend for themselves.

a2767.speaker: Yusuf Luqmaan, father displaced from Lower Shabelle due to drought
a2767.speech: "I've moved from several camps, and each time I saw the route of aid deliveries, whether food or materials like shelter and mattresses, they were redirected. After several days, we see the same supplies being sold in the markets." ; Explained that his daily work involves digging holes and burying rubbish, for which he earns a mere dollar per day, but that he often goes home empty-handed: "Sometimes, I don't get work at all."

a2767.speaker: Small business owner at Hamarweyne market (anonymous)
a2767.speech: Revealed that he buys ready-to-use therapeutic food with the logos of international aid groups from individuals who obtain the supplies from humanitarian agencies, and emphasised that he does not have a direct connection with the original suppliers; the therapeutic food items, typically meant for malnourished children, are being sold for $30-$35 per carton.

a2767.speaker: Sahro Sharif Mohamed, mother of nine displaced from Jowhar
a2767.speech: "My child was supposed to receive 35 pieces of biscuits per week, but I only get 9. Four or five of them I sell to feed the rest of my family, leaving my child with just 4."

a2767.speaker: Anbiya Isaac, displaced woman
a2767.speech: "There was a time I went for three days without food, and I did not receive any form of assistance - not even water."

a2767.speaker: Mohamud Ma'alin Abdulle, Chairman of the Disaster Management Agency
a2767.speech: Confirmed that aid diversion is a known issue and that investigations are currently underway: "We are aware of this issue, and it's a possibility since aid passes through many hands. We are conducting a large-scale investigation into the situation."

a2767.speaker: Aid agencies (non-response)
a2767.speech: Attempts to contact aid agencies for comment on the diversion issue were unsuccessful, as they were unable to speak with the reporters.

a2767.speaker: Shafi Sharif Mohamed, researcher and chairman of the Somali Researchers Association
a2767.speech: Warned of the disastrous consequences that could unfold: "The situation could worsen beyond expectations if the aid does not reach the people. This could lead to a greater need for food and resources, further exacerbating the situation, with devastating consequences for the Somali population."

a2807.speaker: Bernard Chiluzi, Old Mutual Malawi's Financial Education Manager
a2807.speech: According to Chiluzi, prioritizing needs over wants is crucial in navigating these uncertain times. "Focus on essential expenses like food, rent, utilities, and school fees," he advises. "Temporarily reduce spending on entertainment, dining out, and luxury items." ; recommends diversifying income streams by exploring alternative sources of income, such as small businesses or temporary work: "Diversifying your income streams can provide additional financial security during uncertain times." ; suggests having open conversations with family members about the situation and exploring ways to cut costs together.

a2807.speaker: Old Mutual Malawi
a2807.speech: has stepped in with valuable tips to help Malawians mitigate these challenges, and believes that by taking such proactive steps to manage finances and reduce stress, Malawians can better navigate the challenges posed by Trump's Freeze on US Aid.

a2807.speaker: US President Donald Trump (Executive Order)
a2807.speech: ordered a 90-day break in what is termed an Executive Order on re-evaluating and realigning United States Foreign Aid.

a2811.speaker: Jeanne Shaheen, U.S. Senator
a2811.speech: has called on Congress to re-authorize the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) to continue saving lives around the world; said despite the overwhelming success of the program, PEPFAR's efforts to protect millions have been impaired by the termination of foreign assistance and dismantling of USAID. "The current administration has made many empty promises and assured Congress that the life-saving humanitarian assistance of PEPFAR will continue. But the reality is, PEPFAR funds remain on hold or have been cut entirely." ; "As we reach the deadline to re-authorize PEPFAR, key provisions are set to expire today - provisions that require that 50% of total funding go towards treatment and that 10% go towards helping orphans and vulnerable children." ; "The time to act is now. Congress must work together to re-authorize this bipartisan program for a full five years and send a clear signal to the Trump Administration that America will not back down from our commitment to save lives."

a2811.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a2811.speech: has warned that South Sudan is among 8 countries in the world to run out of Antiretroviral therapy drugs in the coming month due to disruption in the global HIV program.

a2811.speaker: Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General
a2811.speech: said the affected countries are facing substantial consequence of the U.S. cessation on funding to foreign countries; said the disruption in HIV program could undo 20 years of progress which would lead to potential rise in prevalence and fatality.

a2811.speaker: National Empowerment of Positive Women United (NEPWU), non-profit organization in South Sudan
a2811.speech: In February 2025 revealed that around 70,000 people have been directly affected by the 90-day suspension of U.S. foreign aid.

a2811.speaker: Mama Evelyn Letio, Executive Director of the National Empowerment of Positive Women United (NEPWU)
a2811.speech: said the PEPFAR program used to donate $1 million annually to the organization and accounted for 75% of the organization's budget; revealed that within an estimated number of nearly 200,000 people living with HIV in South Sudan, nearly 70,000 rely on international assistance; said the suspension threatens to reverse years of momentum gained in fighting the pandemic.

a2860.speaker: Emmanuel Assilamehoo, National Director of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO)
a2860.speech: Said that the international environment at end-December 2023 remained characterised by good growth prospects despite geopolitical tensions, explained by the fall in oil prices and continued control of inflation worldwide; that economic activity within WAEMU maintained its momentum with GDP growth projected at 6.5% in 2024 against an estimated 5.7% in 2023, and that inflation came out at 3.7% in 2023 and should reach 2.5% in 2024 ; Said Benin's real GDP growth is estimated at 6.1% in 2023 and projected at 6.0% in 2024, and that the inflation rate came out at 2.7% in December 2023, after 2.9% a month earlier, and should reach 1.6% in 2024; he notes that this downward trend results from the combination of support measures taken by the Beninese authorities to contain prices, good performance of the agricultural sector and the monetary action of the Central Bank

a2860.speaker: Emmanuel Assilamehoo, National Director of the BCEAO
a2860.speech: Indicated that the central bank notes with satisfaction that banking activity indicators maintained their growth momentum during the 2023 financial year, notwithstanding an economic environment marked by the effects of the closure of the borders with Niger and the removal of subsidies on petroleum products in Nigeria; total assets consolidated by 8.3% to 6,418.9 billion CFA francs against 5,924.5 billion at end-December 2022, and bank loans grew by 17.2% to 3,079.9 billion against 2,627.4 billion in 2022

a2860.speaker: Emmanuel Assilamehoo, National Director of the BCEAO
a2860.speech: Explained during the press briefing that full repatriation of export earnings by companies not only allows primary banks to have sufficient resources to finance the economy, but also allows the BCEAO to increase its liquidity supply to the banking system

a2860.speaker: Officials of the two institutions (BCEAO national directorate and APBEF-Benin)
a2860.speech: Stressed that participants in the consultation meeting noted that the quality of the local loan portfolio continued its improving trend, with a gross portfolio deterioration rate of 4.8% at end-December 2023 against 7.2% a year earlier, below the Union average of 8.7%

a2860.speaker: Participants in the BCEAO/APBEF-Benin consultation meeting
a2860.speech: Welcoming the encouraging results obtained in the national banking system in general, noted that room for progress remains regarding the homogeneity of individual gross portfolio deterioration rates around the national average, as well as the banks' own cash position, whose deficit remains at a rather worrying level ; noted that the rate of repatriation of export earnings by economic operators came out at 81.4% (the standard being 100%), resulting in a repatriation shortfall valued at 80.5 billion CFA francs for 2023

a2860.speaker: Lazare Noulekou, President of the Professional Association of Banks and Financial Institutions of Benin (APBEF-Benin)
a2860.speech: Reiterated, during the meeting with the press at the end of the first consultation meeting between the two parties, APBEF-Benin's commitment to strengthen monitoring actions in collaboration with the national directorate of the BCEAO as part of the follow-up of companies in default with the export-earnings repatriation framework

a2964.speaker: Dato Saravanan Karathihayan, chargé d'affaires of the Embassy of Malaysia in Guinea
a2964.speech: “Guinea holds a special place in Malaysia's heart as a privileged trading partner in West Africa,” before underlining the historic ties and the complementarities between the two economies.

a2964.speaker: Chaloub Yolande Colle, Deputy Director General of the Private Investment Promotion Agency (APIP)
a2964.speech: Insisted on the strategic purpose of this framework of exchanges: “This meeting symbolizes much more than a simple gathering. It embodies our shared determination to build a concrete, lasting and mutually beneficial partnership. We are among people of action, and that is what gives our meeting its full meaning.”

a2964.speaker: Dato Saravanan Karathihayan, chargé d'affaires of the Embassy of Malaysia in Guinea
a2964.speech: According to him, trade between the two countries saw significant growth in 2024: Malaysian exports to Guinea rose 91.2%, reaching 50.6 million USD; Guinean imports rose 750.7%, that is 290 million USD, dominated by agricultural and mining products.

a2964.speaker: Malaysia
a2964.speech: Also reaffirmed its commitment to education and the digital economy, two key axes of its development strategy, with numerous study scholarships available for young Guineans and training offered through the Malaysian Technical Cooperation Programme (MTCP).

a2964.speaker: Ibrahima Sory Sylla, director of LUBA Technologie
a2964.speech: Welcomed the initiative: “After my studies in Malaysia, I always wanted to create this link of cooperation. Today, this dialogue gives a real opportunity to Guinean youth to connect to international markets and know-how.”

a2964.speaker: Mohamed Salif Touré, CEO of Hydro Plus Solution
a2964.speech: Shares this optimism: “This event allows us to build concrete bridges between Guinean and Malaysian companies. It is a space for giving rise to joint projects.”

a3046.speaker: Ministry of Agriculture, Environment and Fisheries of Mozambique
a3046.speech: announced today (29) that the country produced 99,200 tonnes of chicken and 23.2 million dozen eggs in the first nine months.

a3046.speaker: Roberto Albino, Minister of Agriculture, Environment and Fisheries
